title: A Nobel for New Keynesian macro, at last!
gist: Noah Smith explains that the year's Economics Nobel to Bob Hall and Mike Woodford vindicates New Keynesian macro, tracing how rational expectations, sticky prices, forward guidance and Woodford's simple model became central-bank standard. He argues the 2021-23 'immaculate disinflation' was the theory's real acid test.

insights.claim: The 1970s stagflation pushed economists from aggregate correlations like the Phillips curve toward microfounded models built on technology, preferences and expectation formation, since correlations break down when policy changes.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Policy relationships that rely on past correlations are fragile; model-based expectations matter for forecasting policy effects.

insights.claim: Rational expectations treats consumers and businesses as on average as smart as the economists modeling them, so policy cannot systematically trick them.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Markets and households price in announced policy, so surprises are what move behavior.

insights.claim: Bob Hall's 1978 paper found that lagged income did not predict changes in consumption, implying people plan ahead and policymakers can influence behavior today by making promises about the future.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Supports forward guidance as a policy tool; policy must be understood by the public to work.
insights.locator: In 1978, Bob Hall wrote a very influential paper

insights.claim: Hall's 1978 result had a caveat: stock prices did predict future consumption changes, so the pure theory did not hold exactly.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Equity prices carry information about future consumption, a link worth keeping in mind for macro nowcasting.
insights.locator: Hall did find one variable that predicted future changes in consumption

insights.claim: Real business cycle theory fails because productivity booms do not line up with economic booms and because it implies monetary policy cannot affect the real economy, contrary to the best evidence.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Monetary policy matters for real activity, so central-bank decisions deserve weight in macro positioning.
insights.quote: monetary policy “is as effective in bringing prosperity as rain dancing is in bringing rain.”

insights.claim: New Keynesian economics emerged in the 1990s and 2000s mainly to explain how monetary policy affects the real economy, focusing on why prices and wages adjust slowly.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Sticky prices and wages are why demand shocks cut output and jobs instead of prices.

insights.claim: Hall's 2005 paper modeled slow wage adjustment, explaining why downturns lead to layoffs rather than wage cuts.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Wage rigidity links demand slumps to unemployment, shaping how severe recessions get.
insights.locator: In a 2005 paper, Hall made a model

insights.claim: Mike Woodford synthesized the many New Keynesian ideas into a simple model, using Calvo pricing and a central-bank interest-rate rule, which became the standard tool of central banks worldwide.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The model underlies how central banks reason about rates, so its logic helps anticipate their reactions.

insights.claim: The simple New Keynesian model implies central banks can cause a short-term recession, as Volcker did in the early 1980s, and can cushion demand drops by cutting rates, but cannot permanently raise employment by keeping rates low.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Rate policy moves cycles, not long-run employment; expect no free lunch from permanently low rates.
insights.locator: This simple model provides a guide for monetary policy

themes.theme: Zero lower bound, forward guidance, QE and fiscal multipliers

insights.claim: After 2008-09, rate cuts to zero were insufficient, leading to three remedies: forward guidance, quantitative easing, and fiscal stimulus.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Know the toolkit central banks and governments reach for when rates hit zero.

insights.claim: Hall's 2009 paper put the government-purchases multiplier at roughly 0.7 to 1.0 normally, and perhaps around 1.7 when the nominal interest rate is at its zero lower bound.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Fiscal stimulus is most effective when rates are pinned at zero and the central bank does not offset it.

insights.claim: Woodford's 2011 analysis shows sticky prices allow larger multipliers, a multiplier well above one is possible at the zero lower bound, and the size depends crucially on the monetary policy response.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Stimulus effects depend on whether the central bank accommodates or offsets them.
insights.locator: And Woodford wrote a paper in 2011

insights.claim: Smith notes the Fed kept rates ultra-low in the late 2010s and even in 2021 as inflation surged, suggesting sluggishness in the Fed's reaction function may substitute for forward guidance and act as an automatic stabilizer.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A slow Fed reaction function can itself anchor expectations, though it risks inflation overshoot as in 2021.

themes.theme: Post-pandemic disinflation as the acid test

insights.claim: Inflation fell from a 9% spike in 2022 to about 3% in early 2023 after Fed hikes without the large unemployment rise seen in the early 1980s.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The soft-landing disinflation shows credible commitment can cut inflation at far lower real-economy cost.

insights.claim: The likeliest explanation for the immaculate disinflation is that once businesses believed the Fed would do whatever it took, they stopped raising prices, so only a clear commitment and forward-looking expectations were needed rather than demand destruction.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Central-bank credibility is an asset; it lowers the cost of future tightening cycles.
insights.quote: All it required was a clear Fed commitment, and forward-looking expectations

insights.claim: Since 2022-23 New Keynesian theory looks more clearly able to shape the future rather than just describe the past, which Smith suspects helped win the long-overdue Nobel.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Expect New Keynesian frameworks to keep dominating central-bank thinking.
